html:
Overview, machinery, and pathways

Acetylcholine is the brain’s most ancient neuromodulator, yet a surprisingly small contingent of cells creates its influence. In the human forebrain only about 400,000 cholinergic projection neurons-barely 0.002% of all cortical neurons-arise from four basal-forebrain nuclei (Ch1-Ch4) and nevertheless blanket the neocortex, hippocampus, and amygdala with arborisations that branch thousands of times before terminating; equally sparse populations in the pedunculopontine/laterodorsal tegmentum (PPN/LDT) innervate thalamus and midbrain, while a single giant interneuron class provides the striatum’s intrinsic cholinergic tone. This "wire-by-volume" organisation means that a single spike volley from one nucleus basalis neuron can modulate on the order of one square millimetre of cortex, setting the gain of tens of thousands of local pyramids and interneurons 1, 2.

The acetylcholine system operates through two fundamentally different receptor architectures that provide complementary computational capabilities. Nicotinic receptors function as ionotropic ligand-gated ion channels, assembled as pentameric structures that open within milliseconds of acetylcholine binding, allowing rapid sodium, potassium, and calcium flux 3. The neuronal nicotinic receptor family includes multiple subtypes formed from combinations of α\alpha2-α\alpha10 and β\beta2-β\beta4 subunits, with α\alpha7 homomeric receptors showing particularly high calcium permeability and rapid desensitization kinetics-properties that make them ideal for detecting transient acetylcholine signals. Muscarinic receptors, by contrast, operate as G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) with five subtypes (M1-M5), where M1/M3/M5 couple to Gq proteins to increase intracellular calcium via phospholipase C, while M2/M4 couple to Gi/o proteins to decrease cAMP. This dual signaling architecture allows acetylcholine to simultaneously mediate fast synaptic transmission and slower, more sustained neuromodulatory effects across different spatiotemporal scales.

Astrocytes express both receptor families and, when activated, alter local blood flow and glymphatic clearance, linking cholinergic tone to metabolic homeostasis 4. A human study relates cholinergic density to brain-fluid dynamics (Figure). The study tests cholinergic lesions in mice (Figure).

The brain’s cholinergic system is organized into two major projection systems with distinct anatomical origins and functional specializations. The basal forebrain cholinergic system, originating from the medial septum/diagonal band of Broca (MS/DB) and the nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM), provides the primary cholinergic innervation to the entire neocortex and hippocampus 5. Recent evidence reveals this system is far more topographically organized than historically appreciated, with specific cholinergic cell populations targeting distinct cortical areas and layers. The MS/DB neurons specifically innervate the hippocampus via the septo-hippocampal pathway and are critical for spatial memory, while NBM neurons project to cortical areas and support object recognition and working memory 6. The second major system consists of brainstem cholinergic neurons in the pedunculopontine tegmentum (PPT) and laterodorsal tegmentum (LDT), which project both rostrally to the thalamus and basal forebrain, and caudally to the pontine and medullary reticular formation.

Signaling expected uncertainty

In cortical circuits, acetylcholine increases the influence of feedforward sensory input while suppressing intracortical and feedback connections, effectively increasing the signal-to-noise ratio and making neurons more responsive to external stimuli rather than internally generated patterns 7, 8. This mechanism, demonstrated through both slice physiology and computational modeling, suggests acetylcholine acts as a network state switch between externally driven "encoding" modes and internally driven "consolidation" modes. A review proposes pathways linking reward and attention (Figure). The review proposes a second cholinergic attention pathway (Figure).

Computationally this corresponds to signalling "expected uncertainty," complementing noradrenaline’s "unexpected uncertainty." In the hippocampus high cholinergic tone during exploration biases the network toward pattern-separation and encoding, while low tone during quiet wake or non-REM sleep favours retrieval and consolidation; medial-septal bursts are phase-locked to theta, timing synaptic plasticity windows across the trisynaptic loop. PPN/LDT bursts gate REM sleep and reset locomotor microstates, whereas their tonic activity tracks vigilance. In striatum, single-spike cholinergic "pauses" or "waves" sculpt sub-second dopamine release, adjusting the credit assignment landscape for habit learning and behavioural flexibility 9, 10, 11, 12. Microdialysis studies in behaving animals show acetylcholine release in prefrontal cortex increases by 140% during sustained attention tasks, with transient acetylcholine release specifically signaling the detection of behaviorally relevant cues 13, 14. The basal forebrain cholinergic system appears to implement a hierarchical attention control system, with prefrontal cortex detecting task-relevant stimuli and then enhancing sensory cortical processing through cholinergic modulation (among other mechanisms) 15.

Seen through a world-modeling lens, acetylcholine switches the brain between two computational regimes: an externally oriented, high-plasticity "model-updating" mode and an internally oriented, energy-efficient "model-exploiting" mode. By modulating sensory gain, hippocampal encoding, and cortico-striatal learning thresholds, this single molecule orchestrates when organisms should trust their generative models, when they should revise them, and how strongly new evidence is written into synapses 9.

Several engineering principles emerge from the cholinergic system’s design. First, the dual receptor system (ionotropic vs metabotropic) allows multiplexing of fast and slow signals through the same neurotransmitter, maximizing information bandwidth. Second, the topographic organization combined with local and volume transmission enables both specific and broadcast signaling modes. Third, the rapid enzymatic degradation provides precise temporal control while the spatial distribution of degrading enzymes creates structured acetylcholine gradients. Fourth, the system implements gain control through multiple mechanisms: presynaptic autoreceptors, receptor desensitization, and activity-dependent synthesis. Finally, acetylcholine’s interaction with other neuromodulators (particularly dopamine) creates a multi-dimensional control space for behavioral states, with different combinations producing distinct computational modes optimized for encoding, consolidation, attention, or action selection.

But how did evolution "bake in" this ACh function (as an architectural bias)?

Topology: a small cholinergic system with diffuse, targeted projections gives a single global variable ("this context is learnable but noisy") the ability to reconfigure many cortical areas simultaneously–a cheap control channel with high leverage.

Receptor diversity = pathway-selective gating: fast nicotinic effects can amplify feedforward thalamo-/cortico-cortical input, while muscarinic effects can reshape recurrent dynamics and plasticity windows, letting "precision" be applied selectively (e.g., to sensory evidence vs. internal recurrence) rather than as a blunt arousal signal. More specifically, muscarinic (M1, M2) and nicotinic receptors are distributed with higher density in cortical layer IV (the thalamocortical input layer) than in upper layers carrying lateral/feedback connections 16. This means ACh release preferentially amplifies feedforward sensory signals while relatively suppressing recurrent top-down predictions.

Phasic signaling for moments of learnability: brief cholinergic transients aligned to cues/outcomes let the brain mark exactly when information is worth incorporating ("this bit is diagnostic"), enabling time-local learning-rate spikes instead of slow, global modulation.

Hard-wired inputs to ACh nuclei: basal forebrain receives convergent inputs from prefrontal cortex (task statistics, uncertainty estimates), amygdala (salience signals), and brainstem arousal nuclei (novelty/salience), enabling a genetically scaffolded estimator that can then be tuned by experience.

In terms of the ACh system’s training data (what trains basal-forebrain ACh release policies):

Inputs (features): convergent streams that summarize cue reliability, attentional demand, and current context 17, 15, 18, including (i) sensory/cortical evidence about whether a cue is present and how diagnostic it is (salience, SNR, ambiguity), (ii) cortical performance-monitoring / uncertainty proxies (e.g., sustained conflict, unstable cue-outcome mappings, rising residual error despite effort–signals that "more evidence + plasticity might help"), and (iii) motivational/state variables (arousal, threat, hunger, reward expectation) routed via limbic/hypothalamic and related afferents into basal forebrain.

Outputs (actions): region- and moment-specific phasic cholinergic transients (plus slower tone) that (a) boost bottom-up impact / cue detectability, and (b) open local plasticity windows–i.e., "allocate precision + learning rate here, right now." 19, 20, 5

Error signals (credit assignment / what counts as ’good’ ACh deployment): the cleanest empirically supported "label" is reinforcement feedback / reinforcement surprise: identified basal-forebrain cholinergic neurons show rapid, phasic responses to reinforcement feedback (including unexpected outcomes) 21, 22, consistent with a broadcast that marks moments when updating is valuable. That reinforcement-linked teaching can then shape–via plasticity within basal forebrain circuits themselves–which sensory/contextual patterns should trigger future ACh pulses (including cases with delayed reinforcement, where basal forebrain learns to bridge cue -> later outcome).

Under this view, basal forebrain is not "given" learnability labels; instead it is trained to emit ACh when doing so increases future reward and/or future error-reduction, making reinforcement-surprise and task-improvement act as an implicit proxy loss for "deploy precision/plasticity where prediction error is compressible."
